topic: Theme F: Religion, Human Rights & Social Justice
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation). They raise different problems for theism
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. Its sub-distinctions (moral/natural, logical/evidential) shape which theodicies are even relevant — and a generic answer misses the structure of the argument.

items.title: Nicaea was a political project as much as a theological one
items.claim: Constantine convened the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE. What was his primary motive?

options.text: Pure theological inquiry into the nature of Christ
Political unity — the empire had recently legalised Christianity, and the Arian controversy was fracturing the church
To remove gospels he personally disliked from the Bible
To suppress the worship of Mary

items.reveal:
Constantine had legalised Christianity by the Edict of Milan (313). The Arian controversy (was the Son co-eternal with the Father, or created?) threatened civil order. Constantine wrote to Bishop Alexander and Arius effectively telling them to stop arguing.

The Council produced the Nicene Creed and condemned Arius. Constantine was baptised on his deathbed in 337 — by an Arian bishop. Theological disputes continued for decades; Athanasius was exiled five times.

The Council did NOT decide the canon of Scripture (a persistent Dan Brown myth).
items.why: Doctrines aren't formed in a vacuum. Constantine wanted a workable state religion. The metaphysics of the Trinity took shape under that pressure — neither invalidating it nor making it 'pure theology'.

items.title: The Eightfold Path has three groups: wisdom, conduct, discipline
items.claim: How is the Eightfold Path structured?

options.text: Eight factors in three groups: wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — practised together, not sequentially

items.reveal:
The Eightfold Path (ariya atthangika magga) is the content of the Fourth Noble Truth. The three groups (panna/sila/samadhi — wisdom, ethics, mental discipline) reinforce each other.

'Right' (samma) means complete or perfect rather than morally correct in a narrow sense. Right View includes understanding the Four Noble Truths; right intention includes renunciation and non-cruelty.

Right Livelihood excludes specific occupations: trading in weapons, living beings (slavery), meat (butcher), intoxicants, poisons. Right Mindfulness is the practice that secular mindfulness movements have isolated from its Buddhist context.
items.why: The Eightfold Path is not a sequential checklist. The three trainings work together — and modern adaptations (secular mindfulness) often extract one element from a framework designed to be integrated.
